messages:
Maya Patel: heads up — Enterprise account ACME-42 is seeing 429s intermittently on our Dedicated pool even though they bought reserved capacity. Customer says it started after a marketing spike around 1:20pm UTC. They sent a few request ids: req_9a3f, req_b7d1, req_c2f4.
Samir Cho: thanks — can you paste the sample response headers and a minimal repro curl? 429s usually mean token-bucket exhaustion or per-tenant shaping. Also which pool_id are they pinned to?
Maya Patel: pool_id is pool-nyc-3, tenant id acme-42. Quick curl they ran (from their report):
```
curl -i -H "Authorization: Bearer xxxxx" -d '{"input":"generate"}' https://api.redwood.ai/v1/generate
HTTP/1.1 429 Too Many Requests
x-rw-rate-limit: 1000/60
x-rw-rate-remaining: 0
x-rw-rate-reset: 38
content-type: application/json
\n{"error":"rate_limited","message":"Throughput cap exceeded for pool:pool-nyc-3"}
```
Eli Torres: I pulled the console metrics — pool-nyc-3 has configured throughput_cap=1200 rps but reserved_pool_commit for acme-42 is 800 rps; autoscale is turned off for that pool. The traffic spike pushed total pool usage to 1125 rps and our per-tenant scheduler dropped ACME back to 800 causing their requests to hit the per-tenant limit.
Maya Patel: oh — so their dedicated reservation is lower than the pool cap? They expected isolation.
Samir Cho: quick primer: Reserved pools guarantee capacity only up to the tenant's reserved_commit. If pool-level loafing/oversubscription happens, we enforce per-tenant shaping to preserve the SLA for committed tenants. Looks like acme-42's commit is 800 rps; marketing spike had many small concurrent bursts which consumed the pool burst budget.
InfraBot: [alert] pool-nyc-3 burst_capacity=0, burst_window_s=60, current_pool_consumption=1125 rps, pool_threshold=1200 rps.
Priya Nair: customer billing note — ACME purchased reserved capacity of 800 rps with burst add-on disabled. They have the enterprise plan but didn't opt into temporary burst credits.
Eli Torres: repro steps I used from a workspace to replicate: 1) spin up 50 parallel clients hitting same tenant key at 50rps each 2) observe cumulative 2500 rps, 3) pool-level throttling kicks in and per-tenant remaining goes to zero -> 429. Example stress snippet: 
```
# run with GNU parallel
for i in {1..50}; do while true; do curl -s -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" -d '{"input":"hi"}' https://api.redwood.ai/v1/generate >/dev/null; done & done
```
Samir Cho: what we should do next: 1) ask customer if they can spread traffic (ideal short-term). 2) If they need instant relief, increase their reserved_commit or enable burst credits on pool-nyc-3. 3) Recommend client-side jittered exponential backoff and 429 handling with Retry-After header. 4) Investigate autoscale policy — enabling burst autoscale would have avoided hard 429s in this case.
Maya Patel: customer is pushing for immediate fix. They want us to enable a temporary burst or raise their commit for the day. Is there a self-service toggle in Console we can use?
Eli Torres: yes — console -> Pools -> pool-nyc-3 -> Edit -> Burst capacity (temporary credits) OR adjust tenant reservation. Also redwoodctl supports admin updates: 
```
redwoodctl pools update pool-nyc-3 --throughput-cap 1400 --burst-capacity 400 --burst-window 60
redwoodctl tenants update acme-42 --reserved-commit 1200
```
Samir Cho: note: changing reserved commit will require billing approval for overage/commit change. Burst credits can be applied instantly for short windows. For SLA alignment, recommend setting tenant reserved_commit >= expected p95 concurrent rps and enabling pool burst_capacity > 0.
Priya Nair: if we bump their commit retroactively we'll need to patch their contract and issue pro-rated invoice. For a short-term emergency, I'll approve a burst credit grant for 4 hours — @samir can you apply and monitor?
Samir Cho: on it. I'll add 300 burst credits to pool-nyc-3 for acme-42 and watch the metrics. Also enabling per-route QoS so heavy background routes don't steal burst. Will post back with results.
Maya Patel: thanks — also let's add a short runbook entry in support wiki: how to check pool vs tenant commitments, typical 429 patterns, and quick CLI commands to apply bursts. Customers keep thinking "dedicated" means infinite headroom.
Eli Torres: logging suggestions for support: ask for last 100 request ids, provide sample 429 headers, and capture Console -> Pool -> Metrics snapshot (1m granularity). That makes postmortem and billing reconciliation easy.
Samir Cho: update — burst credits applied at 1797010300. ACME reports error rate dropped to <1% within 90s, p95 latency normalized. I'll keep monitoring for 30m and then we can decide whether to increase permanent commit. :thumbsup:
Maya Patel: perfect. I'll follow up with the customer on next steps and documentation. Thanks team.
